A vision encoder emits feature vectors that generally do not match an LLM's input distribution or width. A learned linear/MLP projector maps those vectors into language-model embedding space, often treating them as visual prefix tokens. This is the simplest bridge and retains many visual tokens. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485)

BLIP-2's Q-Former uses a small set of learned queries to extract a compact representation from frozen visual features. Flamingo uses a visual resampler and gated cross-attention inserted into the language model. [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12597) [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198)

$$Z_{visual}\in\mathbb R^{N\times d_v}\ \longrightarrow\ Z_{bridge}\in\mathbb R^{M\times d_{LM}}.$$

Smaller $M$ reduces language-model attention cost but can discard fine print and spatial detail. OCR, high-resolution tiling, video sampling, and multimodal instruction data determine capabilities beyond the bridge architecture itself.
